steps.user_message: I want to file my 2024 taxes correctly. I'm single in Atlanta GA. W-2 from Coastal Manufacturing: $96,500. Additional income: $18,400 (freelance writing, 5 clients), $2,650 from Barclays, $420 from Schwab. Home office: 170 sq ft exclusive; I pay $1,880/month for 740 sq ft. Deductions: $5,100 student loan interest (Great Lakes, 2018–2021); $1,500 to Salvation Army have the receipt; $1,050 unreimbursed expenses. Can you tell me what I can deduct, whether to itemize or take the standard deduction, how to treat the home office, and what forms I need?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Short answer up front
- Most likely you should take the standard deduction for 2024 (almost certainly better than itemizing with only $1,500 of charitable gifts and no other big deductible items you reported).
- Your freelance writing must be reported on Schedule C (and Schedule SE for self‑employment tax). The home‑office deduction is available for the freelance work (not for your W‑2) and you can choose either the simplified method ($5/sq ft) or the actual‑expense method (your allocable share of rent/utilities/etc.). With the numbers you gave, the actual method (allocating rent) will almost certainly give you a larger deduction than the simplified method if you have no other home expenses to allocate.
- The “student loan interest $5,100” needs clarification: only interest you paid in the 2024 tax year is potentially deductible, and that deduction is capped at $2,500 and phases out at higher incomes. Based on your combined income, you will very likely be over the phaseout and therefore ineligible for the student loan interest deduction unless your 2024 MAGI is much lower than the rough estimate below.
- Necessary federal forms: 1040, Schedule C, Schedule SE, Schedule 1 (for adjustments), Schedule B (because your interest/dividends total > $1,500), and Form 8829 if you use the actual home‑office method. Possibly Form 8995 (QBI) — see below. State return (Georgia) also required.

I’ll walk through the details, show approximate calculations, and list the forms and next actions.

1) What income you must report
- W‑2 wages from Coastal Manufacturing: $96,500 (reported on Form 1040 from your W‑2).
- Freelance writing: $18,400 — report on Schedule C (gross receipts), minus allowable business expenses.
- Barclays ($2,650) and Schwab ($420): treat as interest/dividends (you should receive 1099‑INT/1099‑DIV). Because combined interest/dividends > $1,500, you’ll use Schedule B.

2) Home‑office treatment (only allowed for self‑employment)
- You said the home office is exclusive use, 170 sq ft of a 740 sq ft rental. That percentage = 170/740 ≈ 22.97%.
- Two methods:
  a) Simplified: $5 × 170 sq ft = $850 deduction (no Form 8829).
  b) Actual: allocate actual home expenses (rent, utilities, homeowner insurance if applicable) by that percentage. You stated rent $1,880/month → annual rent = $1,880×12 = $22,560. Allocable portion for the home office = 22.97% × $22,560 ≈ $5,182. (If you have utilities, renter’s insurance, etc., allocate those as well and add them.)
- Form to use: Schedule C to report business income and expenses. If you use the actual method, use Form 8829 to compute the allowable home office portion (this feeds into Schedule C).
- Important rules: Home office must be used regularly and exclusively for the business. You cannot use the home office deduction against your W‑2 income — it reduces net self‑employment income only.

3) Self‑employment tax and effect on AGI
- Self‑employment tax (Social Security + Medicare) applies to net earnings from self‑employment. You report it on Schedule SE. You may deduct half of the self‑employment tax as an adjustment to income on Schedule 1.
- You also get a potential Qualified Business Income (QBI, Section 199A) deduction of up to 20% of your qualified business income from the Schedule C (Form 8995 or 8995‑A may be required). With your level of income, you are likely under the threshold where complicated wage/property limits apply, so you’ll likely qualify for roughly 20% of the net business income (after business deductions) — that’s an additional tax reduction to consider.

4) Student loan interest ($5,100)
- Only interest you paid in tax year 2024 is deductible on Schedule 1, up to $2,500.
- The deduction is phased out based on MAGI (modified AGI). Given the incomes you listed, your MAGI will very likely exceed the phaseout limit for single filers, so you will probably not be able to take this deduction. (If the $5,100 refers to interest paid in prior years rather than interest paid in 2024, you cannot deduct those earlier‑year payments on your 2024 return at all.)
- Action: confirm the year(s) the $5,100 was paid and provide the 1098‑E (student loan interest statement) for 2024 if you have it.

5) Charitable donation $1,500 and “unreimbursed expenses $1,050”
- Charitable cash gifts to qualified charities are deductible if you itemize (Schedule A). You reported $1,500 — that alone is well under the 2024 standard deduction for a single taxpayer, so itemizing only for that amount is not beneficial.
- “Unreimbursed expenses” — since 2018, miscellaneous employee unreimbursed expenses are not deductible for most taxpayers. If the $1,050 are business expenses that were unreimbursed by clients/employers but pertain to your freelance business (office supplies, subscriptions, phone portion, mileage, etc.), they should be reported on Schedule C as business expenses. If they are employee unreimbursed expenses related only to your W‑2 job, they are not deductible.

6) Quick approximate calculations (illustrative)
- Total gross income = 96,500 + 18,400 + 2,650 + 420 = $117,970.
- Two home‑office scenarios (assuming the $1,050 is a freelance business expense; if not, adjust):

  A) Simplified home‑office ($850) + $1,050 business expense:
   - Schedule C net = 18,400 − (850 + 1,050) = 16,500.
   - Self‑employment tax (approx) = 15.3% × (0.9235 × 16,500) ≈ $2,335. Half SE tax ≈ $1,167 (an above‑the‑line deduction).
   - Adjusted gross income ≈ 117,970 − 1,167 ≈ $116,803.
   - Standard deduction (single 2024) ≈ $14,600 → taxable income ≈ $102,203 (before any QBI deduction).
   - QBI ≈ 20% of qualified business income (approx 20% of ~16,500 = ~$3,300) may further reduce taxable income (use Form 8995).

  B) Actual home‑office (rent allocation ≈ $5,182) + $1,050 business expense:
   - Schedule C net = 18,400 − (5,182 + 1,050) ≈ 12,168.
   - Self‑employment tax ≈ 15.3% × (0.9235 × 12,168) ≈ $1,720. Half SE tax ≈ $860.
   - Adjusted gross income ≈ 117,970 − 860 ≈ $117,110.
   - Taxable income after $14,600 standard deduction ≈ $102,510 (before QBI).
   - QBI ≈ 20% of ~12,168 ≈ $2,434 may reduce taxable income further.

- Bottom line from the two estimates: using the actual allocation of rent to the home office yields a noticeably bigger Schedule C deduction than the simplified method, and therefore lowers your net self‑employment income and overall tax.

7) Forms you’ll likely need (federal)
- Form 1040
- Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business) — freelance income and business expenses
- Schedule SE (Self‑Employment Tax)
- Schedule 1 (to report adjustments to income)
- Schedule B (Interest and Ordinary Dividends) — because your interest/dividends total > $1,500
- Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) — only if you use the actual method for home office
- Form 8995 (or 8995‑A) for the Qualified Business Income (QBI) deduction — likely the simple Form 8995
- Schedule A only if you decide to itemize (unlikely with only $1,500 charitable gifts unless you have other itemizable expenses not listed)
- Georgia state return (Form 500) — check GA rules and withholding/credits

8) Recordkeeping and other practical items
- Get your 1099‑NEC/1099‑MISC/1099‑INT/1099‑DIV and W‑2s.
- Keep documentation for the home office (floor plan, photos, lease, rent receipts) and receipts for any business expenses (subscriptions, supplies, software, invoices).
- If you expect similar freelance income next year, consider estimated tax payments (Form 1040‑ES) or increasing withholding at your W‑2 job to cover self‑employment tax and income tax on freelance income.
- Consider retirement options that reduce taxable income (SEP IRA or Solo 401(k)) if you want to lower 2024 taxable income.

9) Questions I need to refine this for you
- Did you actually pay $5,100 of student loan interest in 2024? Or is that a cumulative amount from previous years (2018–2021)? If you have a 2024 Form 1098‑E, what amount is shown?
- Are the $1,050 “unreimbursed expenses” business expenses for the freelance work, or are they employee expenses related to your W‑2 job?
- Do you have any other deductible items not listed (state/local income or real estate taxes paid, mortgage interest, major medical expenses, large unreimbursed casualty losses, etc.)?
- Do you have records for utilities or renter’s insurance for the home (if you want to use the actual home‑office method)?

If you want, I can:
- Recalculate with exact numbers once you confirm whether the $1,050 is business related and whether the $5,100 is 2024 interest.
- Draft a checklist of documents to gather before preparing the return.
- Prepare a step‑by‑step guide to filling in the specific forms (which fields to populate on Schedule C, SE, 8829, 8995, etc.).

Note: This is general guidance based on the facts you gave. For a definitive filing decision and to account for all rules and any state specifics, consider using tax software or consulting a CPA/tax preparer.
